subtopic: H.M. FORCES
H.M. FORCES
speechtext:
1.	What action has the government taken regarding the application made by the medical faculties of Canadian universities for some direct assistance to those medical students who are entering the medical branches of His Majesty's forces?
2.	AVhat representations have been made, by whom and for how many students?

subtopic: H.M. FORCES
speechtext:
I should like to make a verbal answer to this question, because it gives me an opportunity to make a statement with regard to the question of policy in assisting medical students who intend to enlist in the armed services. With regard to part 1 of the question, it is estimated that the armed services will, during the ensuipg fiscal year, require probably 800 medical officers, of which 50 will be needed by the navy, 600 by the army and 150 by the air force. As a matter of fact the army could take on almost at once probably 150 medical officers; and the air force, I am informed, probably 75 to 100. These requirements are being brought to the attention of the medical profession throughout Canada and the Canadian Medical Association is cooperating by sending out a questionnaire to all members of the profession.
I come now to the direct answer to my hon. friend's question. In order to assist in increasing the future supply of medical officers for the armed forces the medical services of the navy, army and air are cooperating in a scheme designed to aid worthy students of medicine who propose to enlist. This arrangement is the result of a thorough study of the medical needs of the armed forces, and has been proposed after consultation with the

medical faculties of the universities throughout Canada. Briefly the scheme is as follows.
The universities will be asked to accelerate their courses, while maintaining the same standard of training, by reducing the normal summer vacation periods to a minimum. In this way a student will be able to cover his full course in a considerably shorter period. By this acceleration of courses students will be debarred from earning in the long summer _ vacation. The plan is designed to make up for this loss of income. It is proposed that the armed services will enlist students at any time during the two final years before they qualify for a licence to practice. They will thus, during this period, become members of the armed forces and will then be granted leave with pay and subsistence allowance which will enable them to complete their courses and to obtain a licence to practise.
This assistance to medical students who intend to join the armed forces will be supplemented by the Department of Labour, in cooperation with the provincial governments, by extending the present system of scholarships. These scholarships, up to a maximum of perhaps $300 per year, will also be open to other worthy students who because of the acceleration of the courses will be deprived of the opportunity to earn during what would be the normal vacation period.
The students who will be eligible for these scholarships will be those who are in need of such assistance, who possess good academic standing and who give satisfactory assurance toN serve in the national war effort in the capacity in which they have been trained.
There will also be some expenditure involved in connection with additional costs to universities on account of the accelerated courses.
The Department of Labour is now in correspondence with the provincial governments with a view to enlisting their cooperation in implementing this extended plan. I may say the provincial governments, or at least some of them, have already cooperated in connection with the plan for scholarships, which is already in force.
In the result, medical students who intend to join the armed forces will, after the first year, receive assistance from the Department of Labour, in cooperation with the provincial governments, by way of scholarships, during the earlier years of their courses, and during the last two years they will receive pay and subsistence allowance as duly enlisted members of the armed forces.
That is the answer to the first part of the question. The second part of the question is:
What representations have been made, by whom and for how many students?

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, March 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley that the house go into committee on a resolution to provide for granting to His Majesty sums not exceeding $1,000,000,000 to assist in enabling the government of the United Kingdom to defray expenditures incurred in Canada for war purposes, and to provide for a loan to the government of the United Kingdom of $700,000,000 without interest.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before adjournment yesterday I was pointing out that this group was wholeheartedly behind the proposal to give to Great Britain one billion dollars' worth of goods. Moreover, I urged that this should be carried further so that there might be an agreement between the allied nations under which their total resources would be put into a common pool for a united effort without incurring debt as between themselves. I justified this proposal on moral grounds, and I stressed the fact that to carry it out in the most equitable way possible it would be essential for each one of these nations to maintain its production at a maximum level, to curtail all non-essential services and to be satisfied to endure a standard of living no more than sufficient to ensure its people a state of health and efficiency.
This proposal is merely an extension to an international basis of what we have been

War Appropriation-Mr. Quelch
advocating on a national basis. We have urged in the past, and we still urge to-day, that the dominion government should be given the, credit to finance its war expenditures without incurring debt, and to drain off any surplus purchasing power through taxation rather than by the sale of bonds.
Under the proposal before the house we are giving to Britain a credit of one billion dollars to buy Canadian goods, but to-day we are not draining off the total amount of purchasing power by taxation but are using to a large extent public issues of bonds. However, we realize that the government is not supporting this proposal on moral grounds.
Under the present system the repayment of large war debts embarrasses both the creditor nation and the impoverished debtor nation. What appears to be worrying the Minister of Finance is how if we become a great creditor nation will the people of Canada be able to buy the goods accepted in payment of war debts. It never seems to enter the minister's head that the people of Canada could be given a credit to buy these goods in just exactly the same way as we are making a credit available to Britain for this billion dollars' worth of goods. Under a balanced economy, one in which the physical demand of the people was made effective against the total production of the country, this would be no problem. As a matter of fact it would be regarded as a great blessing. It would be merely a question of making the physical demand of the people effective against the production of the country. This might be done, if there were unemployed, by instituting large-scale public works projects, by increasing the amount of old age pensions, and by paying pensions to people who were physically incapacitated. Or, on the other hand, it could be accomplished by putting into operation a price discount on the sale of goods in exactly the same way as to-day we apply the sales tax for the opposite purpose.
While we support the principle of giving these goods to Britain we are not in accord with all the provisions of this resolution. I shall leave clauses 2 and 3 of the resolution to discuss at the committee stage, but I want now to refer to clause 4, which reads:
4. That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money not exceeding in the whole the sum of one thousand million dollars ($1,000,000,000) as may be required for the purpose of defraying the expenditures and making the purchases referred to herein, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.

We are opposed to the general principle of that clause. We believe in the principle of financing the war without incurring debt. We believe, and the minister himself has admitted time and again in this house, that the real cost of a war is met while the war is being fought, met by the loss of lives and the destruction of property and war materials. We cannot see why, if the real cost of the war is met during the war, we should allow any financial costs to be left to be paid afterwards. In other words, we are saying that we want to have the right to consume goods during the war but we also want the right to issue claims against future generations for the payment of these goods. We maintain today, and we have maintained consistently since the declaration of war, that if people can go through the war maintaining a decent standard of living and come out of it no worse off than they were at the start, they should consider themselves indeed lucky. It would be advisable, no doubt, to allow the purchase of a limited number of interest-free war savings certificates so that people may be allowed to put aside a certain amount of money to take care of certain eventualities; in other words, put aside a little for a rainy day. Therefore we urge again that to the extent that taxation and the sale of interest-free war savings certificates fail to meet the government's expenditures the services of the Bank of Canada should be utilized. When I say that, I do not use the expression "interest-free", because it makes little or no difference what the rate of interest in that case would be, because all profits of the Bank of Canada come back to the people and therefore the interest charges also come back after all expenses are met. I maintain that under such a proposal there would actually be far less danger of inflation than under the present method, because the Minister of Finance has admitted that fundamentally the main reason for taxation and the sale of bonds is to curtail the spending of the people, to withdraw money from circulation.
What actually happens when bonds are sold? You may see high-pressure salesmen persuading people to buy bonds who in reality are not in a position to buy them, and the result is that within a short space of time a certain number of these bonds are resold to the chartered banks. When these bonds are sold to the banks, the banks create the money with which to buy them, so that the very purpose which the government is trying to accomplish by selling bonds is defeated by the chartered banks in creating that new money.
Not only that, but in the 1941 victory loan campaign $135,000,000 was created by the chartered banks for the purpose of lending

War Appropriation-Mr. Michaud
to people to buy bonds. There you have, on the one hand, the government selling bonds in order to withdraw money from circulation, and on the other hand, you have the chartered banks creating $135,000,000 of new money with which to buy those bonds, thereby defeating the very thing the government is trying to do. As time goes on, undoubtedly more and more of these bonds will be sold to the chartered banks, which in effect will be inflationary.
On the other hand, if you were financing this war on a true pay-as-you-go basis, withdrawing all surplus purchasing power from circulation by taxation, it would not be possible for the chartered banks to expand the amount of money in circulation by the purchase of bonds from the people.
In closing, I should like to say that we do appreciate the fact that step by step the government is being compelled1 to recognize the soundness of so many of the things which we have been advocating in the past. For instance, consistently from 1935 to 1939 we propounded the principle that anything that is physically possible and desirable should be made financially possible. To-day nobody would dispute that principle, which was ridiculed time and again during those five years. To-day, however, the government never misses an opportunity of emphasizing the fact that no financial restrictions of any kind whatsoever shall be allowed to impede our war effort. I only hope for the benefit of the people of Canada as a whole that the government will continue that policy after the war and tell the people then that no financial restrictions of any kind whatsoever shall be allowed to impede our peace effort. But already, I am afraid, we are being told by people in high places that when the war ends the screws will be put on and people must be prepared to tighten their belts and cash in on their war savings certificates to provide the money to take them through the depression which many people seem to think s inevitable after the war.
Another thing we advocated time and again was that when there is a condition of unemployment it is possible to have a creation of money for the purpose of providing full employment by a further expansion of the production of the country; and again we were invariably met with the cry of "inflation". But the very first declaration of the Minister of Finance, then acting minister of finance, in this house when he was discussing the war policy was that there would be monetary expansion for the purpose of providing employment and expanding our resources. If it is sound to have monetary expansion for the
purpose of providing full employment in order to develop the resources of the nation at war, surely it should be just as sound to do the same thing in peace, in order to raise the standards of living of the people.
Another point. When we advocated monetary reform in the past we were often accused of supporting something of an inflationary nature. However we always stressed the need for price control. I dealt with this last session. The minister himself ridiculed in past years the idea of price control; yet to-day we have it.
Lastly, as to making goods available to Britain without debt, let me assure the minister that we in this corner will be only too pleased to cooperate with him at any time he finds it necessary or desirable to do those things which we have been advocating consistently in the past.

I never claimed that we had not that right, but we shall be freer to make such arrangements. I would refer the house to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said yesterday, as reported at page 1420 of Hansard, beginning with the last paragraph at the bottom of the left hand corner:
The continuance of these purchases and expenditures, however, involves a continuance of the huge deficit of the sterling area in its balance of payments with Canada which must be financed (very largely at least, perhaps wholly) by Canada itself. We have realized for some time that the accumulation of sterling balances which, as I have explained, was the most important method of financing this deficit, was appropriate only as an interim or transitional form of financial assistance. It involved the growing up of what was nominally a demand liability by Britain to Canada, the future of

War Appropriation-Mr. Michaud
which was bound to involve uncertainties, particularly as the amount grew far beyond anything which could be repaid by Britain in Canadian dollars except perhaps over a very long period of time. Moreover, the indefinite growth of this obligation, if permitted to continue for years, would have led to the existence after the war of what would be in effect a huge and unmanageable war debt owed by Britain to Canada.
I am sure that hon. members can recall the grave international problems and difficulties which arose in the nineteen-twenties and nineteen-thirties from the huge international war debts which had grown up during and immediately following the last great war. Here it is necessary to emphasize the distinction between a domestic debt and an international debt. Domestic debts involve payments between one person and another in the same country and give rise to no problems of currency and exchange. International debts, on the other hand, can be settled only by the transfer of goods and services from the debtor country to the creditor country. Such transfers can be made, only if and to the extent that the creditor country is prepared to accept goods and services from the debtor country for not only principal repayments but also annual interest charges. In other words, the creditor country must be prepared to see an increase in its imports or a decrease in its exports, or both. Experience has shown that countries will accept these payments in the form of imports only to a limited extent on balance, if at all. To do so, of course, exposes their producers to more intense competition from abroad and the excess of imports serves as a deflationary influence which appears to be unwelcome in normal peace times. On the other hand, the inability of debtor nations to make payment when the creditor nation will not readily accept imported goods and services in payment, is bound to lead to international misunderstandings and frictions. Consequently, there is a practical limit to the amount of international debt which can be satisfactorily carried and repaid, particularly when such debt arises from the economically wasteful processes of war. The experiences of the last twenty-five years are too well known for me to labour this point at greater length.
It is to avoid this situation that the lease-give proposals have been made to Britain and have been accepted. What are the implications of these proposals? They imply that we shall have balanced our indebtedness; that each country will owe to the other as much as the other owes; that there will be no accumulated debt in sterling or accumulated credit in sterling to our account in London so as to compel us, to obligate us to accept in payment goods which might come into conflict and competition with similar goods manufactured in our country. My hon. friend saw that point yesterday and clearly elaborated on it, and in this regard we are agreed. That was why I concluded my argument on the occasion I spoke in Quebec by saying that we should have to avoid purchasing, or that we should no longer have to import, from Britain, things
that our own workmen can produce. I meant that instead of making a loan to Britain of so many million dollars in sterling for certain goods, munitions of war, supplies, foodstuffs and so on, instead of asking them to make a deposit of sterling to our credit in London to that extent, we would be better off if we made a free gift of these goods, not being obligated after the war, during the period of post-war construction, to accept goods in payment- and this for the reasons mentioned by those who have already spoken.
The leader of the opposition at page 1427 of Hansard, expressed his misapprehension of what might happen if we had to take merchandise in payment of indebtedness to us which had accumulated on the part of Britain. He said:
The effect of the two operations is not greatly dissimilar for the time being at least. In neither case are we sending actual money.
That is perfectly true, as we are trying to get the Canadian people to understand. We are not sending one billion dollars in dollars to Britain when we make this gift. The money remains in Canada and we are sending goods, munitions, supplies, foodstuffs and so on. The leader of the opposition continues:
It is retained in Canada and gives employment to Canadians. But, as the minister has pointed out, the real difference will be apparent in the post-war period when the problem of final settlement of all war debts will arise.
And later on:
Of course I agree that it depends on what kind of goods they are. We must visualize the acceptance of some goods

I am willing to go with the minister that far.
I agree with that; but what I said at Quebec was that after this war we must try to avoid, as far as possible, accepting from other countries goods that can be manufactured in this country, in order that we may give employment to our returned1 soldiers and our workmen who are now employed in war industries.

and President Franklin Roosevelt on August 14, 1941. The fourth paragraph of that charter reads:
They will endeavour, with due respect for their existing obligations, to further the enjoyment by all states, great or small, victor or vanquished, of access, on equal terms, to the trade and to the raw materials of the world which are needed for their economic prosperity.
' I might also support my statement by the text of the lend-lease pact, signed on February 23, 1942, and also to support the conclusions I drew in the closing portion of my remarks at Quebec city. First let me read part of the first paragraph of the preamble of the lease-lend pact:
Whereas the governments of the United States of America and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland declare that they are engaged in a cooperative undertaking, together with every other nation or people of like mind, to the end of laying the bases of a just and enduring world peace securing order under law to themselves and all nations . . .
Then I go on to article VII:
In the final determination of the benefits to be provided to the United States of America by the government of the United Kingdom in return for aid furnished under the act of Congress of March 11, 1941, the terms and conditions thereof shall be such as not to burden commerce between the two countries, but to promote advantageous economic relations between them and the betterment of world-wide economic relations. To that end they shall include provision for agreed action by the United States of America and the United Kingdom, open to participation by all other countries of like mind, directed to the expansion, by appropriate international and domestic measures, of production, employment and the exchange and consumption of goods, which are the material foundations of the liberty and welfare of all peoples; to the elimination of all forms of discriminatory treatment in international commerce, and to the reduction of tariffs and other barriers; and, in general, to the attainment of the economic objectives set forth in the joint declaration made on August 12, 1941, by the president of the United States of America and the prime minister of the United Kingdom.

Now, by way of conclusion, I wish to repeat what I have said privately and1 publicly, outside this house, that this proposal of a gift of a billion dollars' worth of munitions, war supplies and foodstuffs to Britain is simply a contribution by Canada to the general war effort, which we should be proud to make and proud to foe able to make, under the present circumstances. Not only will it react to the benefit of our senior partner, Great Britain; it will react to the benefit of Canada herself; and we should have no apology to make and no excuse to offer for this so-called gift. subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to see introduced the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) respecting the gift to Great Britain. That is one of the most creditable acts, as far as the government is concerned, since the war started. During the last few years before the war when w.e relied on status and all that, hardly a single member in the front government benches appeared to believe in the British empire.
The resolution refers to the war, and certainly the war overshadows every other subject. Nothing else matters to-day, notwithstanding the fact that we have many domestic problems which have had consideration for almost forty days since the beginning of this session. But those domestic matters amount to nothing; if the war is not won, life will not be worth living in this country.
The resolution is divided into four paragraphs. In my opinion primary matters should come first, and for the remainder of the session we should have a war session. That is what has happened in England. Anyone who will read the English daily Hansard will find that from the first to the last of their sessions the discussions have related entirely to war matters. While in England they have many gigantic domestic problems, problems connected with rehabilitation and matters of that kind, the government over there realizes that those matters must wait until after the war.
Notwithstanding what has been said this afternoon by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud), on trade and commerce and markets, Canadians know the truth, and they know in their very bones that everything we have in this country in the way of defence, freedom, civilization and liberty we owe to the mother country and to no other agency. We threw away our defences and our friends, with the result that when war broke out we were back to where we were in 1812, in a condition of complete dependence on the mother country for all the protection, security and freedom we enjoy to-day. The hour has now come when the people of Canada and other parts of the empire must decide one great question. They must decide whether Canada will resume its place as one of the senior partners in the empire, and as a senior dominion supporting the mother country in its fight for freedom and salvation of religion and of the world, or whether we shall be content to be blotted out for all time, and content to permit our empire and all it has stood for through the ages to fall, as have other empires in the past. We read about
what happened in the days of Greece and Rome, and we must ask ourselves whether we are content to wither away. Heaven forfend that this empire should ever pass away like that, because it is before the world to-day as one of the main, last bulwarks of Christianity, freedom and liberty.
I say this because we must remember that parliamentary institutions were firmly established, for all time after the first meeting of the Reformation parliament. Then two little islands at the edge of Europe leaped up and became a great nation, a pioneer in freedom and civilization and liberty, the world over, with the right to worship God as one pleased. The great growth which has taken place from those days of Elizabeth; the inventions of medicine and science; the development of art and the glory of Elizabethan literature-the growth of all these things was phenomenal. The English bible was translated into many languages the world over. Great Britain became the pioneer, the protector of the weak, as she spread the principle of freedom throughout the world. The new world in America owes her a debt of gratitude they can never repay before God. Since this war began, she stands clearly as the trustee for a better world.
The first paragraph of the resolution deals with the billion dollar belated gift, as it is called, to the mother country. The second paragraph refers to the $700,000,000 Great Britain has now spent on war in many ways in Canada, and provides an exchange rate for refunding at $4.45 to the pound sterling. This sum is to be without interest until the end of the war. The third paragraph gives the governor in council power to purchase some unmatured securities and for the repatriation and refunding of these securities. A guarantee is given, and in my view this is a most commendable form of financial aid to the mother country. The fourth paragraph deals with the financing of the billion dollar gift, and makes provision for the payment of any expenditures on interest.
In his speech the minister referred to that paragraph in the speech from the throne which states:
You will also be asked, as an integral part of Canada's direct war effort, to approve a contribution to Britain of vast quantities of munitions, foodstuffs and supplies.
In the second paragraph of the resolution the means have been provided, The sum of $700,000,000 for war purposes owed in Canada is mentioned and the rate is given and this debt taken care of. There is a further stipulation that there shall be no interest until

War Appropriation-Mr. Church
after the termination of the war, and this debt also, I hope, will in time be cancelled as a second gift-it is long overdue.
I was keenly interested in the question raised the other night by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) with respect to the failure of the government of the day to give the country proper information respecting the public war expenditures and the public accounts. That information has been given in the mother country in detail daily to parliament. Over there they have a committee on national expenditures. It meets during the greater part of the year, and through its efforts all expenditures are coordinated, and a huge reduction in capital and maintenance charges made, and a check on every cent spent.
I said back in 1938 that Canada should establish food reservoirs then in the old country to take care of our exportable wheat surplus, something which would have given the mother country, when war broke out, a great advantage and reservoirs there for Canadian canned goods, cheese and other foods and textiles. However, nothing was done about my suggestion, frequently made before the war. The other day my leader referred to what the Hon. H. A. Wallace, Vice-President of the United States, and former secretary of agriculture, had to say in connection with pooling allied food reserves.
The history of courage in this war has been gloriously rewritten on land, on sea and in the air by the wonderful youth of Canada, on active service the world over and on the seven seas, many of whom raced to England to enlist. If we look at the cause and effect in connection with this resolution, we see at once a need for greater coordination and cooperation with Great Britain in new methods of production and man-power to aid her. A billion dollars is said to be a large sum of money, but when in finance you get away up in the sky and in the clouds in figures like that they become so staggering that the larger the sum the less likelihood there is that it will be well spent or that there will be any drastic control over it.
We are entitled to more real information. We are entitled to know the long-range war policy of the government, because since the war started Canada has been given less information than has any other dominion. Certainly we are given less information than are the people of Great Britain. Democracy in Canada cannot be saved by refusing to face facts and by refusing to tell the people the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth about our war effort. As I said here on March 21, 1939, before the war, if the people of Canada and

the other dominions are not given the facts; if they are allowed to know only as much as their rulers will permit them to know, then those people are embarking on a course fraught with a financial condition leading in some instances, as it will in Canada, to bankruptcy.
I believe in the wisdom of telling the people the great danger and peril at our very door and gate. In future let us tell them the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about the whole war and about the danger on the Atlantic and Pacific seaboards, and the real facts, building up from the worst of these facts.
Yesterday some reference was made to our sister industrial province of Quebec. I believe one of the desires and the will of the people of Canada from coast to coast is that sooner or later, before the war is over, that great country of France may rise again and be restored to her place for freedom in all history. She was our great ally in the last war, and 4,000 sons of Toronto, who helped to defend her in the last war, are buried there, sleeping their last sleep until the resurrection morning. I hope enough support will be given against the axis powers to restore that great land to the glory it enjoyed in the past history of the world as one of the great democracies.
We in Canada should be a united country from coast to coast. Wolfe and Montcalm lie buried together at Quebec, and the inscription on their monument attests the unity of the races in this country, as described in the motto on their memorials on the Plains of Abraham. Britain and France in the last war fought for a better world and for a better fate than has befallen them. I have always believed in the principles of confederation since I have been in this house-of the old Cornish battle cry of "each for all and all for each." There is no use in our thinking that this is going to be an easy victory. We have no divine right to victory. This is going to be a most difficult, hard and heavy task and we should face that fact before it is too late. Facts are facts, and we should take our lessons from the past. So far we have lost the war and almost every battle; we have had no successes except some in Libya, and one or two others.
The money to be voted by this resolution will help in a small way to restore confidence in the mother country as to what the dominions are doing to aid her in her hour of greatest peril. One thing that makes the vast expenditures under this resolution necessary is the fact that after the great war Great Britain and France, the two great democracies, threw away their defences. Not only did they

War Appropriation-Mr. Church
throw away their defences, they threw away their friends. These two leading nations listened to the pacifists and those who pleaded that there should be friendship for Germany, that country which has put 20,000,000 men, by beastly war and savage mechanism, under the sod of Europe in the last three generations. These two great nations, Britain and France, disarmed at great cost, thus causing this war, and now this resolution is necessary in order to help the mother country to save the world and civilization. If the truth were told, Munich was necessary. As I said in the house last year, Munich was necessary because the two great democracies, Great Britain and France, were obliged to buy an armistice on terms which were humiliating because together or singly, Britain and France were in a helpless state and even they were no match for the greatest aggressor of all history, Germany.
That was not Hitler's fault. I suggest that it was the fault of Great Britain because she listened to the babble of the pacifists and decided to disarm, urged on to do so by Canada and the United States. I should like to give all praise to the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Churchill, who spoke in this chamber only a little over three months ago, with you, sir, presiding so ably. As he said himself the other day, he considers himself a servant of the House of Commons, a child of the House of Commons. If he is a child of the House of Commons, then he is a child who is beloved and respected the world over for what he has done in this emergency after Dunkirk, although he is being blamed to-day because there have been some reverses, as war always brings. History shows that the great Prime Minister Pitt and Napoleon also had reverses. You must expect reverses if you go to war, but Britain and her brave and faithful allies will yet smash the axis powers.
However, something should be done by the government of the day on a greater production effort in Canada. Lord Beaverbrook is to come to Washington shortly. As I said the other day, he is a native of Maple, Ontario, although he lived in the maritime provinces nearly all the time he spent in this country. He is a great Canadian, and I think his services and those of Viscount Bennett should be used by this dominion at home and abroad in a total war effort. When Lord Beaverbrook comes to Washington he should be consulted by the Department of Munitions and Supply and come to Ottawa to help us about our production. I think I am fair enough to admit that the government should be given a great deal of credit for what they have done since the war started, especially as they did not believe in war or armaments and all that kind of thing. They believed, with the
pacifists, in the League of Nations, disarmament, the Monroe doctrine, the Kellogg and Locarno pacts, collective security and all those pacifist things. It cannot be expected that we would be able to develop an army in a year or so. While our production has been fairly good, it should be three times as large as it is and we shall not have a total war effort until that point is reached.
We are told that our production is to improve, but it may be too late. Hitler seeks to capture the future with what he is doing at the present time. We hope to win the war, but do the opposite by talking of what we will do in 1943. If we are going to do anything about production, we shall have to improve things all along the line. I ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) to bring down a white paper to show us what has been done in the way of production so far, and the long range policy one is out in Britain. We are told that our war production is two or three times as large as that of the last war, but that kind of thing does not mean anything. I submit that the services of Lord Beaverbrook should be sought in this vaster production effort. He should be asked to come to Canada to give us the benefit of his experience. I hope the government will invite him to come here when he arrives in Washington-he was to be here with Mr. Churchill but was sick-and I have no doubt that he will be ready to give this country every assistance.
Shipbuilding should be our first priority. As I pointed out here, two years before the war started, Great Britain had 2,000 fewer ships than she had in 1914, and yet there were 5,000,000 more mouths to feed. Great Britain must import 94 per cent of her foodstuffs and nearly all her raw materials. We made a mistake in the imperial conference of 1937 by not joining New Zealand and Australia in a vast, gigantic empire shipbuilding policy. In 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939 I urged an empire shipbuilding policy and the opening up of all our old shipbuilding plants to build ships to carry necessary food, munitions, wheat and other supplies to the old land.
I believe that our production has been tremendously increased since the last war. Mr. Churchill told the British House of Commons that Great Britain's production was twice that of the United States. The United States to-day is somewhat in the position of Great Britain after Dunkirk. They were not ready, they were not prepared. Great Britain is doing a wonderful work; her production is going ahead by leaps and bounds. Mr. Churchill has said that England's production is four times greater than it was in 1917.

War Appropriation-Mr. Church
We are told that ours is twice what it was in the war of 1914. We might as well say, for all the good it will do, that it is a hundred times greater than it . was during the Boer war, or a thousand times greater than it was during the battle of Hastings.
Before the war started I contended that there were too many in this house with the Geneva type of mind. Pretty nearly all those on the government benches were of that type of mind, as were nearly all the members of nearly all the parties here. They all believed in such shams as the league, and collective security, which is only collective security for the world with an armed Britain. The Minister of Finance and the minister with the high sounding title, the Minister of National War Services, went over to see the Geneva sittings as Canada's delegates, before the war, and they came back thoroughly imbued with the Geneva idea and lack of vision not to have seen the folly of it all. We thought we could do without an army and a navy and retain our freedom, but how under the rise of Hitler in Germany from 1935 was civilization to be maintained without being armed? Take the example of the great disaster in the Pacific. We let Australia down by not supporting her at the imperial conference of 1937. We should have made a grant to the Singapore base for Pacific protection and adopted the Jellicoe report which called for a vast empire shipbuilding policy, for a naval policy, for the training of 5,000 cadets for the navy in Canada and a naval college, and for the building up of a merchant marine, all urged in 1937 by me. In answer to all the pacifists in and out of this house, I say now to them, quoting from Jeremiah, chapter 37, verse 19:
Where are now your prophets which prophesied unto you, saying, The king of Babylon shall not come against you, nor against this land?
As we see how close the axis powers now are to our front door on the Atlantic and Pacific, and the war came in September, 1939.
I am not one of those who both in and out of this house preached such pacifism. Hon. gentlemen before the war were entitled to their pacifist views, and while I have criticized pacifism, the whole world was imbued with that idea for years before the war, and especially the democracies, one of which. France, it is too bad to say, went down and out. But I would say this, that if I was one of those who had changed their views on pacifism after the war broke out, I would far rather have come to the House of Commons and sat on the penitent bench and said that such views brought the world to this terror and disaster, and that I had made a grave mistake. I would not now go around Canada, 
posing as a super-patriot as some of them have been doing. It has taken two months for us to have one word of discussion in the house on our war effort in connection with this resolution to provide money and munitions and food for the mother country. It was the pacifists who caused the war; there is no doubt about that. But for them we would never have had this war and the dislocation and awful disaster of the whole world, and dear knows, no one knows as yet who is going to win the war-nobody knows that fact yet. We had the idea preached to the youth of Canada in schools, state colleges and universities that the profession of arms was demoralizing. The pacifists held that war was wrong, that it was wrong to take life in the defence of one's country; but as a matter of fact they in their taxes were prepared to pay others to join the army and go out and fight when war came and do that very killing act. They did not propose to go to war themselves-oh, no. When war came they would stay home and preach pacifism and say, "now, soldiers, get to the war". Ruskin, himself a man of peace, has spoken about war, and its results in this passage from "The Crown of Wild Olive":
When I tell you that war is the foundation of all arts, I mean that it is the foundation of all the high virtues and faculties of men. It is very strange to me to discover this; and very dreadful, but I saw it to be quite an undeniable fact. The common notion that peace and the virtues of civil life flourish together, I found to be wholly untenable. Peace and the vices of civil life only flourish together. We talk of peace and learning, and of peace and plenty, and of peace and civilization, but I found those were not the words which the muse of history coupled together: that on her lips the words were-peace and sensuality-peace and. selfishness-peace and death. I found, in brief, that all great nations learned their truth of word, and strength of thought in war; that they were nourished in war and wasted by peace; trained by war and betrayed by peace, in a word, that they were born in war and expired in peace.
War in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, will never be abolished in any country of the world until men learn to do their duty to their neighbours much better than they have done in the past. When they do that, war will cease.
There is nothing said in this resolution about two or three matters I want to mention, and one is shipping. How are we going to get these supplies and munitions across the Atlantic ocean? Our great shipping losses have been outlined by Mr. Churchill in the British House of Commons. It is deplorable that the British empire should have suffered the loss of these empire bases off Ireland. It has resulted in the loss of the lives of our brave soldiers and seamen and an awful tonnage. If we had not had these bases in the last war we should have

War Appropriation-Mr. Church
lost that war, and in view of their importance I urge upon the government that something be done to acquire them now or force their acquisition at once.
We are spending nearly $4,000,000 a day on the war, and yet there is hardly one item of war expenditure in the public accounts. Part of that $4,000,000 is being spent by all the various outside bureaucratic control boards and commissions. Does the auditor general audit the accounts of each of these boards in detail? No. Then what check or audit is there upon them, and by whom, as they spend money like water, uncontrolled. Will the government consider the appointment of a select committee of the house on national expenditure, as they have done in Britain? The committee in Britain has done a great deal of good. But the committee on war expenditure here, on which $25,000 was spent, did not find out anything because the first motion they passed was that they should not inquire into past expenditures. They reported here and their report is in the archives. Sooner or later the House of Commons will have to see that they recover at once control over every cent of these huge expenditures.
This resolution also shows the necessity for an empire war cabinet. The war is now all over the Pacific, north and south. Japan is roaming around 15,000 miles there and has the absolute command of the sea. She has submarines which can cross the Pacific without refueling. If you had a million men, as Mr. Churchill said, you could do nothing at all in the Pacific because Japan is moving around all these islands in the Pacific, north and south, and around Australia like a circus and nobody knows which will be attacked next. So I urge upon the government that something be done about a war cabinet to get a united war control and union and empire cooperation at once.
In England a civil war was fought for nearly one hundred years before parliament acquired control of public expenditures, but in this country we lost that control as soon as the war started. These outside boards and commissions can spend what money they like. A bureaucratic form of government has been set up and some 25,000 orders in council have been passed-and parliament meeting here exercises no control over public expenditure. You can hardly find an item in the public accounts that relates to the ivar. Parliamentary control is a myth. The public accounts committee should be meeting, and should be broadened into a committee on national expenditure as they have in England, which has saved the taxpayers millions of pounds by coordinating expenditures. Such a committee should go into details of all ministers' expenditures such.
for instance, as the rates of pay of soldiers. They are most inequitable, and that question should certainly come before such a committee at once, and rates of pay be adjusted. In Great Britain the audit committee has effected great economies, and it would be a great help to the Minister of Finance here to have such a committee examine into government expenditure and apply the big stick of retrenchment. In my opinion the minister is taking too much money out of the taxpayers' pockets, and a large amount is going to be expended under this resolution in refunding operations. Half of the war expenditure does not help beat Hitler at all. Most of the expenditures under the other $2,000,000,000 resolution have already been made and all we can do is to conduct a post mortem on the one or two larger resolutions. We just sit here like a lot of coroners or undertakers inquiring into what has been done in the past, expenditures made over which we had no control and cannot reduce a dollar. Bureaucrats have issued countless orders and spent a huge amount of money to be provided by the taxpayers without parliament having any control over the expenditure or even knowing one iota about them. It is a farce. In my opinion this House of Commons will be open to criticism by history and it will be held up as a reproach to Canada and to this parliament that we sat here and exercised no control over expenditure whatever, if we do not at once take action along that line to force a showdown on it.
Let us not be unmindful of our great heritage as the senior dominion. We have neglected to take the simple precaution of training the youth of Canada to defend their country on land and sea and in the air, which is the first principle of preservation of any democratic country.
I charge the lack of support in 1937 of these things to the account of the government. At the imperial conference the government did nothing in behalf of the tie that binds Canada to the rest of the empire, namely the British navy and merchant marine. We did nothing to promote the building of ships or the putting of the merchant marine on a proper basis.
The authors of the empire trade agreements in 1930-32 conferred a great benefit on this country. Britain has always been our best customer. Other customers come and go but she stays on forever. I have read Hansard since the war started, and, except for the text of this one resolution now before the chair, I have yet to discover in it an iota of praise to the mother country for all she has done for us. She has saved us in Canada from the axis powers and has enabled the vast majority of

War Appropriation

Mr. Church
our youth to proceed with their daily avocations and indulge in their amusements and soprts as though there was no war at all. I am not objecting to their doing so, but their first duty is to their country, and they will live to regret what they are doing. What I object to is that our country is not half appreciative enough to the motherland for the British fleet and the Royal Air Force, but for which we would have been invaded long ago, and the enemy would have come up the St. Lawrence, through the maritimes, the central provinces, the prairies and the west and arrived on the Pacific coast. Not only Canada, but all America owes Britain a debt of gratitude that they can never repay. It is too bad that the Anglophobia so frequently expressed from outside in the press and on the radio is still as before the war, allowed to continue and function. Nothing has done more to kill recruiting.
By this vote we can thank the mother country for giving us, before and during this war, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom of thought, freedom from fear, from famine and from battle, and also from the immediate murder and sudden death which the axis powers would have caused us. We do not half show our appreciation of all this. If Canadians would only stop, halt, listen and think, they would know that but for Britain we would have endured, for nearly two and a half years past, the mechanized hordes of the axis powers with all their savagery, brutality and tyranny. They would have swept through Canada and enslaved us, and we would have had to endure the same treatment as the small countries and larger ones of Europe-the concentration camps, the loudspeaker, the spies, the tramping of feet, the sergeant-major, the gestapo, the whips, the spirit of barbarism, brutality and savagery. But for Britain we on this continent would have been compelled to endure these experiences long ago, while Canada fails to awake and has a policy of everything as usual.
In my opinion there have been too many big stick methods in connection with the government's effort. They use a lot of controllers. The air we breathe is about the only thing that is not under control. These controllers are continually making speeches and radio addresses threatening the tightening of belts, employing other big-stick material, and fastening upon us three or four times as many regulations as they have in Great Britain.
As I understand it, all of us in this house are outright in favour of the war; but I do not think it is fair for any group in this chamber or outside it to use the war for the purpose of discussing their socialistic proposals on domestic questions-the function of money, the basis of credit and that kind of thing.

Surely we can wait until the war is over before taking up these matters. Personally I believe in certain economic conservative principles; I do not favour socialist leadership or the creation of a great national payroll, nor do I believe, with the present peril confronting us, the prosecution of the war should be used to put over all sorts of socialist doctrines, to change the functions of money and alter the basis of trade although I believe in sound money brought up to date for changed conditions. I believe in the right to hold private property. I believe that, even after war, the principle of private ownership will prevail- a principle so strongly held in the days of Macdonald and Laurier, when everybody owned some private property; it might have been only a cow, a small mill, a little store, a small farm or a little shop or industry of some kind. We have been slow to see how all this is passing away in Canada and how the people are becoming proletarians. But I strongly favour the postponement of discussions on these matters until after the war. The right of a small, independent business man to hold private property is derived from nature, not from man, and the state has no right to abolish it, but only to regulate its use. Parliament should abolish half these bureaucrats and not competitive business.
I believe that the Conservative party derives its strongest support from the working classes. We have received the votes of working men and trades unionists, because we believe in protecting industry, the farmer, and labour, and in preserving our own work for our own workmen, our own markets for our own products.
I suggest that a bill be introduced in this house similar to one which passed the British House of Commons on February 17 of this year, to restore pre-war trade practices so that business will know where it stands and can function as formerly. It seems to me that our present policy in Canada now is, "never were there so many who knew so little about so much." That is bureaucratic control for you. That is the principle on which these boards and their controllers are acting. We should beware of this hidden agency of aggression before it is too late; it is one of the things we are fighting against in this war, and the extension of this system not only adds to the burdens of the minister in financing the war but will handicap him when it is over, and ruin all competitive business, great and small, with so many artificial barriers and burdens.
It is a staggering reflection that, for all the blue books and statements relating to parliamentary government and returns, and our public accounts, nobody knows from day to

War Appropriation-Mr. Martin
day how many bureaucrats are carried on. the public payrolls or what they are costing the country. When hon. members ask questions they cannot obtain such information, because the figures are not there, and the treasury cannot give them because they don't know as it is done over their heads. The figures given here to-day are wrong for to-morrow. It is too bad that so much money has been spent over the heads of the taxpayers and their representatives in the House of Commons, who have no say or control.
In conclusion, I suggest that a committee on public accounts should be appointed. I should like to see a levelling up of existing inequalities in the pay of our fighting men on land, on the sea and in the air. I believe that if all hon. members had copies of the rates of pay and allowances and realized the inequalities which are shown in them, there would be a sensation. I hope something will be done to remedy this state of things, and force an immediate inquiry into the pay and allowances of our officers and especially the rank and file of our men and also the women's army.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
In rising to make a few observations, I think that the house will agree, after hearing the speech of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) this afternoon, that he was yesterday put by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) in an unfair light. The leader of the opposition took certain isolated sentences from a speech made by the minister in the city of Quebec and did not relate those observations to the context or to what the minister had in mind. This proposal cannot be looked upon in a narrow sense. It is one which requires a good bit of explanation, particularly in certain sections of Canada- not only in one-and that is exactly what the Minister of Fisheries was trying to do-to indicate, in quarters where there has already been expressed some opposition to this measure, the reasons for it. I think that, having in mind that there was really a common interest between the minister and the leader of the opposition, on reflection the latter might be prepared to regard the minister's contribution as one that deserves commendation, and not the censure which he gave it. Because the fact is that in many parts of Canada the man on the street, as well as the magnates of finance, have expressed some doubt about the wisdom of this proposal, largely because it has not been viewed in its proper perspective.
What is the proposal which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has sought to embody in this resolution? It is to provide Britain with an opportunity of meeting her scarcity or shortage of Canadian dollars by supplying,
without charge or obligation, munitions of war, raw materials and foodstuffs up to the value of $1,000,000,000. As the leader of the opposition said yesterday, there is involved no transfer of money but simply a transfer of goods. How anyone, in the light of the situation in the world to-day, when our smugness of a former day must be dissipated, could oppose this measure, I say frankly I fail to understand-not simply because this is a gift to Britain, not simply because we are giving financial assistance to Britain in a common cause, though that in itself would be a reason for supporting it, but because in view of our experience during the last twenty years, this, since the occurrence of the present war, is the first real statesmanlike endeavour to meet the whole problem of international debt and international obligation.
Every member of this house will recall the period between 1921 and 1928 when the debtor nations found themselves in the ridiculous position of paying back their debts with money which they acquired by way of loans from their creditors; how Germany was able to pay her reparations, thanks to huge extensions of credit by the United States, her main creditor; how Britain, who received moneys by way of reparations from Germany, was able to pay part of her obligation to the United States out of money which she received from Germany, which in turn had come from the United States. That ridiculous tripartite arrangement provoked every man who had given any serious thought to these problems to consider the necessity of putting the whole problem of international debt in its proper perspective. The exclusive policy of certain countries in the period between 1921 and 1928, which refused to have these obligations paid in terms of goods and services, let alone in terms of currency, created a situation which led to that dismal period between 1930 and 1935.
I for one am therefore prepared to support this proposal on two grounds: First, because if we are going to win this war it will be necessary for all of us to look upon this matter in the light of a common obligation, in the light of the need of pooling our resources and the abandonment of our national and sectional interests; secondly, because the Minister of Finance in this proposal has given leadership not only to our own country but to all the nations of the world and in particular to those who will hold a creditor position when the war is over. That is one aspect of the problem. It seems to me, however, that the problem has another serious aspect. This is' assistance to Britain; but Britain is not our only ally. The war has now reached many fronts, and if we are truly the arsenal of democracy, sharing that position

War Appropriation-Mr. Martin
with Britain and the United States, there comes into mind the whole question of priorities in war production and its distribution. Is this aid to go to only one quarter? Is everything we produce to go to Britain alone? Is it simply to go to Britain and Russia? How can we, in view of the fact that we are a Pacific power as well as an Atlantic power, ignore our obligations to our sister dominion, Australia, who at this time is faced with perhaps a nearer danger than any other country in the world?
We know what the news is in the press to-dajr. I do not comment on its merits because I do not know what the merits are, except that I think someone in this house should refer to it. We have the cry from Australia as expressed in one of the leading publications of that country, in the Sydney Daily Telegraph of yesterday:
Whoever is responsible for the allocation of Canada's war output has lost his sense of values. Nobody has suggested that Australia should be given priority. Britain must have the best share of all production; Russia, India, Egypt and China must have a good share. But the flow of production should be dictated by the urgency of the situation in the various war theatres. ... A London Times statement, that the Pacific battle is a race between American reinforcements to Australia and the Japanese advance ignores the fact that Canada is also a Pacific country. Australians simply will not understand why a Pacific country and a sister dominion should be sending nineteen times more war material to Egypt than to Australia. You would imagine that Canada would put first things first. The United States is wholeheartedly committed to making Australia a major base for operations against Japan. She is doing so because she knows that the west coast of America would be wide open to attack if Australia fell. The west coast means Canada. Australia's defeat would mean the end of the British empire in the Pacific. That is why Canada's export figures for February do not make sense.
That is Australia. To that observation the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is reported as saying that the allocation of materials which go from this country and from the United States is supervised by Britain herself. I have no quarrel with that. A war is not run from a barber shop or even from the House of Commons, 'but I do say it is important that there should be some expression of opinion which would give some encouragement to Australia, that this country is determined, in so far as it can, to effect the distribution of the materials of war produced in Canada, consistent with what those in charge regard as in the best interests of our cause.
Yesterday the leader of the opposition related this whole problem of international 
obligations after the war to the kind of world that we were going to have after the war was over, and there resulted in consequence the observation of the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell), in this house, that we had to take account of the future in the light first of all of our mistakes in the past and of what was, he said, the undoubted demand of the vast majority of citizens throughout the world at the present time. He was opposed to the system of free enterprise. He regarded the future as envisaging, if it was to have any sort of order at all, something on a socialistic basis, and the leader of the opposition urged that we should have a system of free enterprise. Then one speaker from the Social Credit party attacked the government because the chairman of the reconstruction committee had expressed the view that the purpose for which we are fighting was to preserve the gold standard, or something of that sort. It is important for someone on this side to express an individual view at any rate, and that I propose to try to do.
In the first place, I think, throwing aside party differences-and that is what I seek to do to-day-and looking at the world from the point of view of the exigencies that will present themselves, we must all be prepared to admit that we are in a transition. I am not so sure that I could accept the doctrinaire attitude of the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, and have a readymade formula for everything that might arise. Nor am I prepared to accept the view of the leader of the opposition that in the world to come we can go on in the laissez-faire manner that we followed in the nineteenth and the early part of the twentieth century. General Smuts, who may be regarded as having some special qualification to speak on these matters; said, in 1941:
Intercourse between the nations will be free, and commerce, economics and finance will be freed from all hampering restrictions and obstructions. As between man and man there shall be social justice; as between nation and nation, there shall be a rule of law, the absence of force and violence, and the maintenance of peace.
Then there was the significant statement of the British foreign secretary, made one month later when commenting on a statement along similar lines by Mr. Cordell Hull. He said:
Institutions and arrangements of international finance must be so set up that they lend aid to essential enterprise and continuous development of all countries and permit payment through the process of trade consonant with the welfare of all countries.

War Appropriation-Mr. Martin
Just to make the record complete, the Prime Minister of this country, speaking at the lord mayor's luncheon in his honour, said:
A new world order cannot be worked out at some given moment and reduced to writing at a conference table. It is not a matter of parchments and of seals. That was one of the mistaken beliefs at the end of the last war.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), I think it was, criticized the government because of the observations of Doctor James, chairman of the reconstruction committee. I think along with that criticism should be taken the observations of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), who, speaking in Toronto in October, 1941, along the line taken by Smuts, Eden and our own Prime Minister, said:
We shall have to develop a kind of government and a kind of economic system that rules out unemployment. No other can survive. Security for the masses . . . must be the first essential of our post-war world.
So when the hon. gentleman talks about this government trying to defend a system that shows so much evidence of imperfection, he is hardly indicting this government fairly or, I was almost going to say, honourably.
What about the future? This whole problem with which we are dealing to-day, trying to adjust the difficulties of debtor and creditor nations in the light of events and circumstances that will, it is hoped, improve the economic condition of the world, will not be met by labels. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say that the world of to-morrow will be socialistic. I must say that I envy them the ability to be comfortable as to the complete adequacy of the point of view which they espouse. But the world of to-morrow possibly will be neither fully capitalistic nor fully socialistic. Surely the system of controls we set up during the period of depression, and elaborated upon during the war, is here to stay, at least for a long time.
I am not saying that the hon. gentleman opposite espouses the doctrine of communism, but I cannot think that communism any longer will have a large group of followers who will support the view that that philosophy is an alternative to war or imperialism. No; if we are to avoid disaster after the war; if we are to avoid the disturbance of national and international economics, strict supervision by the war-time control method over raw materials, foreign trade, foreign exchange, shipping and so on will have to be maintained, along the line of the arrangements that now prevail between the United Kingdom and the United States, and between the United States and Canada. If, for
instance, Canada and the United States are able to cooperate during the war in the matter of control of shipping, exports and imports, raw material supply and the use of balance of payments, it should not be impossible to maintain this type of collaboration after the cease-fire signal is given.
Yesterday the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, commenting on what he said was the lack of appreciation of this problem by the leader of the opposition-and I thought he was a little unfair in that regard-said the time had come when we had to plan our internal economy, when we had to plan the economies of all nations on an international basis. But we in Canada have done that very thing. Our system of price controls; our system of controlling wages, together with the other types of control that we have set up in this country, I venture to suggest represent almost as complete a form of planned economy as one could get in any part of the world. But the great danger is that if you allow that type of planning to proceed on a basis of absolute rigidity, without allowing for some competition between a measure of collectivism and a system of free enterprise, for instance, you will have the very sort of evils which have resulted from totalitarianism itself. So what is required with regard to this whole problem is, I think, not a doctrinaire attitude; not a definite conviction that we have the formula that will solve all these problems; but, first, a recognition that the old order is gone; second, a recognition that laissez-faire capitalism will no longer play the role it has assumed in other days, and that these problems must be dealt with realistically, not on the basis of an idealism which may be desired but which, I venture to suggest, cannot readily be achieved.
To summarize, in so far as guaranteeing a measure of social security is concerned, I would say this. Many of the forms of administrative controls which have become part of the job of government will have to be maintained. Thus far these controls have embraced national economies alone. They will have to receive a wider application. The system of licensing, of banning, of imports and exports; the regulation of exchange rates-all these are among the methods by which these controls have operated; and the greater the control, the greater and more extensive the planning. As I have said, the Canadian price and wage control policy; the control of production; the control of raw and material supplies, and other controls, have given us the type of planning which hon. gentlemen opposite have been urging for years; but now that it is here they refuse to recognize it.

War Appropriation

Mr. Martin

I have tried to deal with this matter as objectively as possible, but I do not want what I have said to be misinterpreted. With regard to what my hon. friend has said about management and labour, there is no point in not disclosing my views on that matter. I have no hesitation at all in saying that collective bargaining is the proper technique by which problems of management and labour should be dealt with. I would go even further than the government has gone in recognizing the desirability of making effective, even by compulsion, a system of collective bargaining. I say that in order that hon. gentlemen may not in Hansard, for others to read, give the impression that I have overlooked the importance of that problem.
The policy of control; the policy with regard to the intervention of the state in these matters, undoubtedly is one that at least charts the course by which the whole problem suggested by this resolution introduced by the Minister of Finance will be dealt with.
There is nothing further to add, except to say this, that it seems to me there is an obligation on the part of members of this house to look upon the proposal in its true light. We are making a gift, true, but a gift which will enure to our benefit just as much as it will to that of the recipients. Second, it is a forward act in respect of the whole problem of debt adjustment which will face the world when this conflict is over.
I say we must be realistic. I know my own views in these matters have undergone definite * changes. But the world is in flames; we can no longer be satisfied with sectional or national interest. Our resources must become the resources of our allies if we are going to bring together that kind of control, for instance, envisaged yesterday in Great Britain by Sir William Beveridge. That is the spirit in which this resolution should be faced. For one, I look upon, the day that is to come not as a day of judgment but as a day of opportunity.

I believe that when the war is over, the people will demand certain things. We are told that we are being governed by order in council, and there is criticism because that is being done in war time. I do not think any orders in council have been passed that have hurt this country very much. If they did, the government quickly took notice of them. I think we shall actually be benefited by the restrictions that are being put in force. Adversity never killed a nation, but luxury and ease are the things that destroy nations. I think one thing the people will ask for after this war is individual freedom. They will want to go back to the old magna charta. War Appropriation-Mr. Lacombe
Nova Scotia and since I came here I have heard a lot about the problems of capital and labour. I do not think capital and labour should be divided into two distinct opposing camps. I think our cooperative effort should not be a class cooperative effort but a cooperative effort by capital and labour, capital representing the savings of the past, and labour representing the efforts of the present. I would not say to this house that we should adopt some socialistic scheme or present some theory as to what capital and labour should do. I would suggest something practicable. I would go to the statute books of Canada and look up the Companies' Act, governing the operation of companies, and I would say that by that law you should elect your directors, part by capital and part by labour. The Prime Minister of this country enunciated that theory many years ago in his book "Industry and Humanity", in which he said there were three parties interested in all industry-the community, capital and labour. Let the community be interested to the extent of making the laws governing business, and let capital and labour be interested together, sitting round a common table in their own right, each doing its part in cooperating to cany on industry, and each having its share. Then all parties will know what is going on, and all will have their rights. None will be exploited either by the leaders of capitalism on the one hand or by the leaders of the trades unions on the other. The majority representing both labour and capital, I believe, would be willing to accept and try that plan, and it would represent a splendid step forward in industry for the future.
I interjected when the leader of the opposition was speaking yesterday on temperance on which subject he made some rather good remarks. By
means of the bill which will be founded upon the resolution now before the house, Canada will purchase $1,000 million worth of goods of various kinds, equipment, raw materials, supplies of foodstuffs, and so on, for Great Britain. All parts of Canada are, I believe, agreed upon this and in favour of this gift, and my purpose in rising at this time is only to point out one thing. I wish to direct to the attention of the house the fact that the purchase price which is. to be paid for these various commodities is; with one exception, to be a cost-plus price. I must express regret at this time that the house has not more details with regard to the quantity of materials available and the respective unit costs of these commodities which we are going to purchase. To get Canada into the production of equipment and supplies we found it

War Appropriation-Mr. Castleden
necessary last year to grant over $100,000,000 to assist various companies in getting into production.
Everyone who realizes that this war will be won or lost on the production lines of the industries of the different countries at war is in favour of the granting of these amounts. We had to get production at all costs, and apparently it is going to be at all costs. Canada was not ready to produce when the war broke out, and all this capital that was required to extend the facilities of production was needed. Canada had to change rapidly from peace-time to wartime production. The thing I want to point out is that practically in every instance costs of production were guaranteed to these companies. Not only were they guaranteed costs of production, but overhead, labour costs, costs of raw materials were taken into account. In practically every instance there were cost-plus contracts, which meant that those engaged in production received cost-plus profit.
It is unnecessary for me to refer to the strike which industry engaged in when it refused to carry out production until it received that consideration. The point is that hundreds of millions of bushels of wheat will be included in this gift, and this is one item in connection with which the producer will not receive even his cost. There is no question about cost-plus. Resolutions that have passed through the house indicate that the price of wheat per bushel will be 90 cents at Fort William, which means that the average farmer will get about 70 cents on the farm. Those who know anything about cost of production, those whose business it is to study and do research work in connection with production costs, agree that the cost is well over a dollar on the farm. It appears to me only logical that if we are to make this gift to Britain, we should do as is done in connection with other commodities that have been supplied, and cost should be guaranteed. Otherwise the farmers can only feel this about it: Canada is making a gift; all the taxpayers are paying their share towards that gift; but those who do the producing, so far as wheat is concerned, will not get their cost. The farmer will bear his share of taxation in the making of this gift; but as regards the one commodity in which he is concerned, and by means of which he is trying to make a livelihood, he is to receive only 70 cents a bushel on the farm for his wheat, whereas wheat costs from $1.10 to $1.20 a bushel to produce. This means that for every bushel of wheat included in the gift to Britain the farmer is making an additional contribution of from 40 to SO cents.
