speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make just a few observations in connection with the resolution under discussion. I must say that I do not see how anyone could oppose a measure that would provide a billion dollars' worth of credit to the people of Great Britain, who for over two years have experienced the hardship and suffering of war. They are a people with great fortitude and, I believe, great faith in the other nations of the British commonwealth. It is only right and proper that we should come to their assistance in times like these, by measures such as those proposed by this resolution.
I do not speak to this resolution as an expert on monetary technique. I do not consider myself such. I am like many others, a mere student, one who has a desire to learn. As I think of this measure in that way, I may get something of a cue from the minister's speech in introducing this resolution in the house, as it appears at page 1421 of Hansard for March 18. He said:
In essence, the proposals are simple and straightforward; but because of the number
r	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mr. Hansell
and nature of the various transactions involved, and perhaps also because they deal in part with matters of exchange, which is a mystery to many persons, the details and perhaps the bill itself may appear complicated to many members of the house.
I was particularly interested in that remark, because I think we have reason to realize that this matter of money, not only internally but externally, as it is related to transactions between one country and another, is sadly misunderstood. It is a subject that does seem to be mysterious; it is a subject that somehow or another has been kept in the dark for a good many years. I recall on one occasion talking to a certain gentleman who, I think, would be regarded as an intellectual; at least he had graduated from a university and had taken some post-graduate work. In talking to him on the subject of money, I asked if he would answer one question; that was, where money came from, how it came into existence. He replied, "Well, of course, if I have a field of wheat out here, that is money." I said, "Do you mean that dollar bills grow on the ends of the stalks?" "Oh," he said, "no, no, no, no, no." Then I said "Well, what do you mean? I asked you where money came from." The only answer he had was, "Well, well, well, well, well." I have asked more than one person the same question, and I have discovered that some people who are quite intellectual and bright have not understood and have not' solved some of the rudiments of this matter known as finance or money.
I was coming east on the train not so long ago and happened to be in the same seat with a man from-well, I will not say where he was from, but he voted for one of the ministers on the government side of the house. When he learned who I was, of course we talked a little bit about politics, and I discovered he was a very good Liberal. He went out of the coach, returned a few minutes later, sat down and said, "Well, Mr. Hansell, tell me: Where is Mr. Aberhart going to get his money from?" So I said to him, "Well, now, Mr. So-and-so, if you will tell me where Mr. Usley gets his from, I think I would1 be in a better position to tell you where Mr. Aberhart would get his." Well, he began to stumble and stew and sweat a little bit, and spit a little bit, and then I began to explain a very few simple things to him. I said, "You see, Mr. So-and-so, it is not social credit you do not understand; it is not Mr. Aberhart's money you do not understand; it is Mr. Ilsley's money you do not understand."
I am quite certain there may be very similar conceptions with respect to a resolution such as this-and, mark you, I have pref-
aced my remarks to-night with a commendation of the government's action in granting to Great Britain this gift of a billion dollars. I think this gift should be made. I am in favour of the resolution. But there are some things upon which perhaps some light should be thrown. The minister has said1 that this is a gift to Great Britain. I wish to compliment him upon his speech in introducing the measure, because it was a good speech. It is couched in nice language; it is clever, and I do not think he misses the mark. But sometimes there is a great danger when one deals in generalities. Sometimes people are past masters of that. I am not accusing the minister on that score, but I must say that when he talks about this gift to Great Britain he uses these words, as they are reported at page 1421 of Hansard,-.
In order to prevent the further rapid accumulation of sterling balances, the government believed that the best course to follow was to make an outright gift to Britain of the foodstuffs, raw materials, planes, tanks, guns and other war supplies which we would send to her, up to the value of $1,000 million.
That is a very carefully worded statement. Then, further down the page we find this:
... I have referred to earlier as the Canadian dollar deficit of the sterling area. This deficit of course arises almost entirely from Britain's requirements for foodstuffs, raw materials, munitions and other war supplies purchased here, so that the proposed gift will, in effect,-
That is a very clever phrase. ,
-take the form of these war supplies.
The gift is spoken of in general terms, and I believe the people assume that it is in reality a gift of foodstuffs, guns, tanks, aeroplanes and war munitions to the British people. What I am asking is this: If it is a gift to the British people of foodstuffs, and so forth, and so on, will the British people receive those foodstuffs free of charge? That is a question which perhaps has not dawned upon many people. The fact of the matter is that the British people will not get those foodstuffs without paying for them.
When I make that statement there may appear to be some confusion of terms. Let me put it in another way: We shall suppose that this billion dollars' worth of goods is sent to Great Britain in 1942. They are all stamped "Made in Canada, 1942". On every can we shall suppose the words, "Made in Canada, 1942", are placed; on every side of bacon, "Produced in Canada, 1942"; on every sack of flour, "Milled in Canada in 1942". This, we say, is a gift to Great Britain.
I have a mother and father living in Great Britain. Am I to expect that my mother

War Appropriation-Mr, Hansell
and father will receive as a gift so many sacks of flour, so many sides of bacon, so many cans of foodstuffs, so much clothing?

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: No.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
My hon. friend over here says no. Then, how is it a gift? That is a question which should be answered. I believe I know the answer, and if my answer is not correct the minister can correct it- for I confessed a while ago that I am only a student, perhaps only an infant, in the study of these matters. There is much that I do not know, and sometimes the mystery seems to me to become a little darker, the further I get into it.
I should like the minister to throw some light on that. We say it is a gift of foodstuffs; and yet when the British people come to get it, they have to pay so much in pounds, shillings, or pence, or whatever the price may be. The fact of the matter is that this billion dollar gift has to be financed from somewhere. Our farmers are going to raise hogs to produce bacon. They are going to grow wheat. They are going to produce the foodstuffs to be canned and sent over there.
I use foodstuffs only as an illustration. They are not going to do that for nothing; they are going to be paid for them. The British people who buy those things in their own localities are also going to pay for them.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
What about giving it to
the army?

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It does not make any difference, technically. I am only using this as an illustration. If it is given to the army, then the British government pays for it, which means that in the end the people have to pay. My hon. friend is only a student.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The British government does not pay for it at all.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Here is an hon. member who says that the British government does not pay for it. Two Liberals disagree. Perhaps my hon. friend over here has not reached the stage of being a student. Let us go on. The fact of the matter is that we are raising in Canada by way of loan a total of one billion dollars from our own institutions. That billion dollars will pay our farmers, our manufacturers or whoever produced the goods. They are shipped to Great Britain and Great Britain is not charged for them. But the British people pay for them just the same. The result is that the British government has one billion dollars more in their treasury.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That is what constitutes the gift.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
That is what constitutes the gift, and I have nothing to say against it.
I am not opposing that. I am simply pointing out that we are raising a billion dollars here to pay our farmers and our manufacturers; we are going into debt to the extent of one billion dollars. The point is that we have taken one billion dollars' worth of debt that Great Britain would otherwise have owed us, and we have converted it into internal debt in Canada which the Canadian people here owe to the banks or whoever create the credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Let me correct that right now. Do not let that idea get abroad at all. The internal debt of Canada will be no larger as a result of this transaction than it otherwise would be. If we were to sell this to Great Britain and take sterling in pay for it, we would have to borrow the billion dollars that my hon. friend speaks about from the Canadian people and take the money and pay the Canadian producers for the goods. But in that event we would send the goods to Great Britain and we would take sterling in return for them. So W'e are not converting a debt from Great Britain into an internal debt in Canada which otherwise would not exist. The internal debt in Canada will not be one dollar larger because we are doing this, nor will the taxes in Canada be one dollar greater than if we were not doing this. I ask my hon. friend to make that clear. I think he understands what I am saying. I want him to make that clear before he goes any further. We are not transferring international debt from Great Britain into internal debt in Canada and thereby saddling our people with a billion dollars of debt which otherwise would not exist. That is not so at all.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I thank the minister for correcting me where I was perhaps wrong in my technical language. I think, however, I am right in saying that there will be no billion dollars of British collateral standing against this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: The fulfilment of a total war creates a debt.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I am being instructed from all directions by the Conservative party.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: You may learn something yet.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I do not think they have corrected anything I have said, although the minister corrected my technical errors. I
.	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mr. Hansell
go a step further and perhaps the minister will correct my technical language here if I am in error. I have not spoken a great deal about the technicalities of our money philosophy because there are other men more capable of doing that. I usually spend my time in speaking on other bills and relieve these men so that they can devote their time to the monetary technique. But 1 have, had to meet these things because of my position in this small party. You meet men every day who ask about these technical subjects.
The point I want to make now is in reference to the prices that will be paid for these goods which are being produced in Canada. Some of these goods will be raised at a loss, especially those produced by the agricultural industry. I do not know how that can be remedied, but I am sure that this billion dollars' worth of credit will not be created at a loss. That is something that is worth considering. These farmers who will be raising these foodstuffs have taxes to pay and other things to buy into the bargain. As they put in their crops or as they attempt to raise their hogs they find they need a line of credit, I have nothing against these institutions. We do not talk against the banks. People get queer, screwy ideas about what we talk about. We have to have money and we have to have credit; the thing is that our banking institutions are doing for us what the government perhaps could do for themselves.
These farmers go to the purveyors of credit and say that they would like to borrow some money in order to produce these goods which are eventually going to Great Britain. They get their loans, but they will have to pay interest. The banking institutions are not going to lose money on these loans. Interest rates will be 4, 5, 6 or 7 per cent; I do not know how much they will want to charge the farmers. So these farmens raise their hogs, wheat or other products and, when they are sold, they find that if they get any profit, it is just a bare profit. I doubt if there is any profit when costs of operation are taken into account. Anyway the financial institutions have advanced the loan and are paid their interest. But they also create the billion dollars and they get interest on that, too. What I am saying is that there should be some responsibility placed upon the financial institutions with respect to this gift to Great Britain. This credit is created at the stroke of a pen; let us make no mistake about that. So I say that they should bear some responsibility with respect to the billion dollar gift to Great Britain.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
We have been here since 1936 and have been propounding and suggesting all along. People have laughed at and ridiculed. our suggestions, but we find that eventually the government goes behind a corner and gets into a huddle and says: "I guess we shall have to do this," do in part what we have been suggesting, because circumstances sometimes force them to do that very thing. We are not seeking to tell the government how to run the country. But we do wish to point out certain things where we think we can be of assistance. I am not opposing this measure.
Reverting to what I was saying about financial institutions bearing some responsibility in this matter, may I refer to the speech made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) this afternoon. He complimented the Minister of Finance and the government, and rightly so, I think, upon giving by this measure what he said was leadership to the world, to those who will hold a primary creditor position after the war. I have no criticism to make of that statement. I think the government is giving some lead in one respect. All that the hon. member for Essex East meant by giving leadership was giving leadership in the cancellation, shall we say, of certain debts owed to Canada by other nations, which might have to be done in any event after the war. That is all right. But where the government is giving more of a lead to other nations is in another part of this resolution, in clause 2, where the government is permitting the $700 million part of the British debt to remain at a standstill, without interest, for the duration of the war. I commend the government for that action. I should like to go so far as to say that perhaps that is what should be done with all foreign obligations throughout all the democratic countries which are fighting together in this war.
There is, however, one matter I would bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance in connection with clause 4 of the resolution, where provision is being made for the borrowing of one billion dollars. On that we are going to pay interest. Would it not be feasible to propose that since this billion dollars of increased debt in Canada is created by our own financial institutions, it should at least be created free of interest? We are taking the

War Appropriation-Mr. Hansell
responsibility of allowing $700 million of British debt to stand without interest to the British people for the duration, but we are asking our own people to pay interest on the billion dollar debt that we are creating for the purpose of giving a billion dollars' worth of goods to Britain. It seems to me, therefore, that the logical thing to suggest is to delete the words ""and interest" from that clause. I do not see why the minister will not do that. I feel that I or somebody else should propose an amendment accordingly to clause 4, perhaps when we are in committee. The minister might do it himself, but I do not think he will.
I do not know what interest will be charged on this one billion dollars, but if the rate were 2 per cent, the interest would amount to $20 million a year. Therefore the Canadian people are going to be, not only in debt to the tune of one billion dollars but, if the rate is 2 per cent, in debt, too, for an additional $20 million of interest every year, and, if the interest is compounded, it will be even more. Why could our own financial institutions in Canada not say: "We will service this at one-half of one per cent, or whatever it may take, and we will create the money without interest."
I am not saying, without debt.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: If I may ask a question, if I pay $10,000 a year life insurance premium to the Canada Life and they lend it to the government, what is going to happen to the profits on that $10,000 which I invest in a Canada Life policy? I am to shoulder the burden, not the institution.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Why should you get any profit on your $10,000?

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Did the bon. member never hear of the sanctity of a contract made before the war?

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I do not want other gentlemen to take up all of my time, but I would answer the leader of the opposition in this way. Perhaps I have been dealing with this billion dollars as a billion dollars of created credit. It may not all be created; I realize that. All I say is that interest should not be charged upon the credit that is created. My hon. friend, even though he be the leader of the opposition, makes no distinction at all between the investment of money which the insurance companies already have and the creation of fresh credit with the stroke of a pen by the purveyors of credit, by those institutions to which parliament has given the right to create credit. There is all the difference in the world between the two. I do not create any money; my hon. friend does not create any money, nor does any
insurance company or any mortgage company. But the banks do create money; that is their function, and I say that when credit is created for the purpose of. servicing a gift to Britain it should be created free of interest charges. Surely that is not asking too much.
I wish to deal with just one other phase of the speech made by the hon. member for Essex East this afternoon. He did not conclude his speech without referring to what the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) had said in respect to the seven-man committee of the government which is now working on post-war reconstruction. In referring to that he said that the hon. member for Acadia was entirely unfair to bring into his speech the fact that Doctor James, the principal of McGill university, who heads the seven-man committee, was of a gold mentality, had been advising the government, and perhaps as an adviser to the government had been advising them along lines that he himself supports- this same gentleman having been sent by the government to Great Britain to consult on post-war reconstruction. The member for Essex East said that the hon. member for Acadia was unfair, and he asked why the hon. member for Acadia did not bring in, ^ for instance, the remarks which the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) made in Toronto.
I should like to deal with that for just a moment, because I assert that there is no essential difference between the remarks made by the Minister of Pensions and National Health, at Toronto or at any other time, and any remarks which Doctor James has made, in connection with post-war reconstruction. Or I will put it in this way: There is not a single, solitary sentence which the Minister of Pensions and National Health has ever uttered on this subject which Doctor James could not support wholeheartedly; he could say "amen to anything the minister said. It seems to me that the hon. member for Essex East was unfair in the observation he made. Doctor James, as chairman of the seven-man committee on post-war construction, is an adviser to the government. I might say in passing that I am still waiting for the minister to say what is the policy of the government in respect to post-war reconstruction. He has not said anything yet. Bringing down bills for soldier reestablishment is not the thing for which this country is primarily looking. It is good in its place; we have nothing to say against such measures; but we are looking for something more.

All right, Mr. Speaker.
In the first place, members of my group and of the organization I represent throughout Canada will favour this gift of a billion dollars; but the cost of this gift is far too great. To judge from the puerile remarks which four or five hon. members have been throwing about the chamber with respect to "twenty-five dollars", I suppose they will never come to realize that this cost is too high until the first thousand years after they are dead; but the cost of this gift is far too great. The minister is making the Canadian people pay double this billion dollars. A good many persons, even in this chamber, do not realize it.

War Appropriation-Mr. Blackmore
In the first place, the Canadian people, in blood and sweat and tears and struggle and effort, are paying the billion dollars. When they produce the beef and the cheese and the wheat they are paying the billion dollars. That is the first thought. The minister himself, in the first days of the parliament, when war was declared, made some statements which indicated that he saw what was going to be the true nature of the effort of Canada. I refer to Hansard of September 12, 1939, page 138, where the minister says:
Whatever such offsets may be, it is important to emphasize that, as I have already said, the real costs of war must come out of current production, out of the goods and services produced during the war.
The Canadian people, in producing those goods, either have paid that cost or are going to pay it in goods. Therefore they pay it once. Then on top of that they are called on to pay for it again, financially, in the form of a debt. The minister will correct me if I am wrong here; I am anxious to get this exactly right. He will tell me this: Is Canada going to be a billion dollars further in debt because she makes this gift to Britain?

speechtext: So the Canadian government is taxing one-half of the money it is now spending on everything-war and current expenses and loans and gifts-and it is raising the rest by borrowing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It is taxing a great deal more than half.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: On over-all expenditures of government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: It takes not very far from half if the assistance to Great Britain is included with our non-war expenditures and our war expenditures during the present fiscal year. But our tax revenues, our total revenues, which are a little higher than tax revenues-because they include post office revenues and certain miscellaneous revenues -are enough this year, or almost exactly enough, to cover our total direct war expenditure-not including our assistance to Britain, or non-war expenditures, but the total direct war expenditure of Canada, which has been met entirely, or is being met entirely, this year out of revenue.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
We would be safe in saying, then, that practically one-half of this billion dollars is being raised by taxation, and one-half by borrowing. If we take it proportionately we are spending this year

about $3,000,000,000 for all expenditures- well, say, $3,500,000,000-of which virtually one-half is to be raised by taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I do not know.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: Well, roughly speaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I shall have an estimate of that in the budget.
Mr, BLACKMORE:	Roughly speaking,
that would be true?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: I do not know what our taxation will be.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
I will go so far as to say that from the evidence adduced so far in the discussions in the house that is the general conclusion that we can draw- that we are raising by taxation one-half of the money it is costing us to carry on, and the other half is becoming a debt against the Canadian people.
On motion of Mr. Blackmore the debate was adjourned.
It being two minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, March 20, 1942
